topicSummary: Kadane's Algorithm (often misspelled as Kaiden's) is a strictly efficient method used to find the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray within a one-dimensional numeric array. It solves the problem in linear time by iterating through the list once, deciding at each step whether to extend the current sequence or start a new one.
learningObjectives: Understand the definition of a contiguous subarray
Recognize the Maximum Subarray Sum problem
Grasp the 'greedy' logic of resetting a running sum when it becomes negative
Calculate the maximum sum of a simple array manually
prerequisites: Concept of positive and negative integers

coreConcepts.name: Contiguous Subarray
coreConcepts.explanation: A sequence of numbers sitting next to each other in the list, without any gaps or skipped numbers.
coreConcepts.importance: Crucial distinction because selecting non-adjacent numbers changes the problem entirely.

coreConcepts.name: Current Sum vs. Max Sum
coreConcepts.explanation: The algorithm tracks two numbers: the running total of the specific sequence we are currently looking at, and the highest total we have seen so far.
coreConcepts.importance: Separating the 'now' from the 'best ever' allows the algorithm to explore new possibilities without losing the best result.

coreConcepts.name: The Reset Logic
coreConcepts.explanation: If the current running sum drops below zero, it is discarded and reset to zero (or the next number).
coreConcepts.importance: This is the heart of the algorithm; a negative running sum will only decrease the value of whatever comes next, so it is mathematically better to start fresh.

commonMisconceptions: Thinking you simply sum all the positive numbers in the list
Believing you must check every possible start and end point (Brute Force)
Assuming the algorithm works for non-contiguous subsequences
Thinking the algorithm fails if all numbers are negative (requires a small adjustment to handle)
realWorldIntuition: Imagine you are tracking a 'happiness meter' minute-by-minute. Some minutes add happiness (positive), some subtract it (negative). If you have a terrible streak where your overall mood score drops below zero, you don't carry that negativity forward; you mentally 'reset' your mood to neutral to see if the next streak of minutes will be better. Kadane's algorithm finds the happiest distinct streak of time in your day.
recommendedFlow: Define the problem: Finding the largest sum of a slice of a list
Show a naive approach: Trying to add just positive numbers (and failing due to gaps)
Introduce the intuition: Why carry 'baggage' (negative sums)?
Walk through the algorithm step-by-step using a small array like [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]
Highlight the moment the sum resets versus when the max sum is updated
